subtype: Approach: comparing with a peer's path without context [Pitfall]
passage:
Indu: You copied a colleague's promotion path?

Gurleen: Every step. Yogesh got promoted in two years: a training course, one big presentation, then a move to the platform team. So I took the same course, gave the same kind of presentation, and asked for the same move. Two years went by. Nothing. I was angry, then confused, and only then did I look at what was different. His team had doubled in size and three senior posts had opened. Mine hasn't grown in years, so there was no senior post to move into. He followed a path that fitted his team. I followed his path in a team where it led nowhere.

qa.q: How long did it take Yogesh to be promoted?
qa.a: Yogesh got promoted in two years.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when nothing happened after two years?
qa.a: Gurleen was angry and then confused, until seeing what was different.

qa.q: What else could Gurleen do to plan a promotion, and why?
qa.a: Gurleen could ask the manager what senior posts might open in this team and build a plan from that, because the path has to fit where the team is heading.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen his own promotion?
qa.a: Yogesh probably saw it as the result of his own effort and did not think about how much the growing team helped.

grounding: Illustrates copying a colleague's promotion steps without noticing that the colleague's team was growing and the narrator's was not, so the same path gives no equal opportunity.

subtype: Approach: comparing with a peer's path without context [Pitfall]
passage:
I sat next to Nikita at the insurance firm for three years, so I saw her plan from the outside.
When Farid was promoted to manager in just two years, Nikita wrote his steps on a sticky note: lead a migration, present at the all-hands, get a certification. She pinned it to her screen.
She did all three within eighteen months. I watched her present at the all-hands, hands shaking a bit but clear.
What neither of us thought about was that Farid had been in the digital team, which doubled in size that year and needed new managers. Nikita's claims team hadn't grown at all. There was simply no manager seat.
When the promotion list came out without her name, she took the sticky note down and folded it very small. I don't know exactly what she felt. She didn't talk much that week.
— Vinita

qa.q: Which three steps did Nikita copy from Farid?
qa.a: Lead a migration, present at the all-hands, and get a certification.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling when she folded the sticky note very small?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed and hurt, since she followed Farid's path exactly and still found no manager seat in her team.

qa.q: What would you change first in Nikita's approach?
qa.a: Before copying Farid's steps, she could ask her manager whether her own team would have a senior opening, and plan around that context or a move.

qa.q: How might Farid see Nikita copying his path?
qa.a: Farid might feel flattered but uneasy, knowing his promotion came partly from his team's growth, which she could not copy.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, someone copying a peer's exact promotion steps without seeing that his growing team created openings hers did not.

subtype: Approach: comparing with a peer's path without context [Pitfall]
passage:
Week one. At lunch, Darshan told Nikita how he'd become team lead in two years: run the internal tools project, mentor two juniors, speak at the tech meet. Nikita wrote it on a napkin. If it worked for him, it would work for her.
Month six. Nikita had finished all three. She was proud of the tech-meet talk. But her manager kept saying, "There's no lead opening on our side right now." Darshan's team had doubled that year; hers had lost two people.
Month ten. The promotion list came out. Darshan's teammate got the new lead role. Nikita wasn't on it.
She found the napkin in her drawer and stared at it. Same steps, different team. She felt foolish for not asking the obvious question at the start: was there even a seat?

qa.q: How much had Darshan's team grown that year?
qa.a: Darshan's team had doubled that year.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when she found the napkin in her drawer?
qa.a: She felt foolish and disappointed, seeing that the same steps could not work in a team with no lead opening.

qa.q: What else could Nikita have tried at the start instead of copying Darshan?
qa.a: She could have asked her manager about openings in her own team and read the promotion criteria, then built a plan that fit her situation.

qa.q: How does Nikita's experience look from Darshan's side?
qa.a: Darshan meant to help, but his advice left out the context of his fast-growing team, so he may feel awkward when her plan doesn't work.

grounding: It shows someone copying a colleague's exact promotion steps across different days without noticing that his growing team offered openings hers did not.
